text: Everything in Chapter 2 so far has used two reference graphs: a single edge and a 4-cycle. This lab hands you a third, slightly different graph -- a 3-node path -- and walks you through simulating depth-1 QAOA on it yourself.

Three nodes, connected in a path: node 1 touches both node 0 and node 2, which aren't connected to each other. The true optimum cut is 2, achieved by putting node 1 alone on one side. Running an exact depth-1 simulation across the gamma-beta landscape, the best result found is an expected cost of about 1.6495, at gamma about 1.052 and beta about 0.393 -- an approximation ratio of about 0.8248, notably better than the 4-cycle's depth-1 ratio of 0.75, because this smaller graph is easier for a single layer to handle well.

The full probability table across all 8 basis states tells the real story. The two optimal assignments, cutting both edges, each carry the highest probability, 0.3345 -- a combined 66.9% of all outcomes. The two 'do nothing' assignments, cutting zero edges, are suppressed to just 0.0098 each. The four cost-1 assignments sit in between at 0.0778 each. A well-tuned QAOA circuit doesn't guarantee a single deterministic answer, but it skews the odds heavily toward the good ones.

If you ran this circuit on real hardware with 1,000 measurement shots at these angles, you'd expect roughly 335 shots on each optimal bitstring, about 78 on each cost-1 bitstring, and only about 10 on each worst bitstring. The practical workflow, which generalizes to every QAOA application in this course including the finance problems in Chapter 4, is: run many shots, keep a running tally of the best bitstring actually measured, and report that as your answer. You never trust a single shot; you trust the best of many.

Chapter 3 now turns to a different algorithm entirely: the Variational Quantum Eigensolver, which shares QAOA's hybrid loop but points it at a different target -- not a combinatorial optimum, but the lowest possible energy a quantum system can have.
